slides.headline: The loop
slides.body: Seven stages. It's the root-cause framework with the stages that only exist when other people are involved.

rows: Stop the damage from spreading: ask people to stop pushing and pulling the affected branch; revoke a leaked credential
none in Git; a message, a provider console
Give every state you may need a name before anything moves
git branch rescue/<what> <id>, git fetch, a copy of a clone
Evidence, at least three hypotheses, one distinguishing command each
git status -sb, git reflog show <ref>, git ls-remote, git range-diff, git log --graph
The change that destroys least and is simplest to undo
Re-run the commands that showed the problem; run the check the affected system runs
Tell the team what to do with their clones; tell the CTO the four answers
Turn the root cause into a control, and write the postmortem
a ruleset, a configuration default, a test, a checklist line

slides.headline: Severity
slides.body: Severity decides who is told and how fast, not how interesting the Git problem is.

rows: A secret that unlocks production was exposed, or wrong code reached production, or shared history is unrecoverable
CTO and security at once; updates on a fixed rhythm
A shared default or release branch held wrong content, or a merged fix was silently lost; caught before or shortly after release
Engineering lead at once; CTO in the summary
A team is blocked or a pull request is unreviewable; no wrong content on a protected branch
The person; nobody else unless a habit needs changing

slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Skipping to recovery. Root cause: under time pressure the destructive shortcut looks like progress, and the loop exists to delay it until the state is known and preserved.
Waiting for the root cause before the first message. Root cause: communication is treated as the end of the loop, when the team needs to know at once which branch to leave alone.
Rating severity by what happened to happen. Root cause: the window is ignored; the level depends on what could have reached users or outsiders while the state was wrong.

Letting colleagues "clean up" their clones. Root cause: a server keeps no reflog, so the history of a server-side branch exists only in the clones, and a pruning fetch, a git gc or a re-clone deletes it.
Reading the generator or the solution first. Root cause: the drill trains diagnosis from an incomplete report, and a cause that has been read cannot be diagnosed again.

beats.text: At some point a message like this arrives. A branch is a named line of commits, the saved snapshots of a project, and main is the branch the whole team shares. The CTO who receives the message doesn't want a command. The CTO wants four answers: what happened, how you know, what you changed and how you proved it worked, and why it won't happen again. Keep those four answers in view. Every drill in this part ends with them.

beats.text: Three of the places are reflogs in each clone: of each local branch, of HEAD, and of each remote-tracking branch.
beats.tele: Three of the places are reflogs in each clone: of each local branch, of HEAD, and of each remote-tracking branch.

beats.text: What the server holds now comes from git ls-remote origin, staged content survives as a dangling blob, and who pushed what is GitHub's record, not Git's.
beats.tele: What the server holds now comes from `git ls-remote origin`, staged content survives as a dangling blob, and who pushed what is GitHub's record, not Git's.

beats.text: No, not by default. The retention periods are Git's defaults, and the lab configuration switches reflog expiry off. And one fact decides how you treat colleagues' clones: a bare repository, which is what a server holds, keeps no reflog unless core.logAllRefUpdates is set.
beats.tele: No, not by default. The retention periods are Git's defaults, and the lab configuration switches reflog expiry off. And one fact decides how you treat colleagues' clones: a bare repository, which is what a server holds, keeps no reflog unless `core.logAllRefUpdates` is set.

beats.text: So the history of a server-side branch exists only as the sum of what the clones remember, plus whatever the hosting platform records. That's why "preserve" includes asking colleagues not to run git fetch --prune, git gc or a re-clone until you've read their reflogs. Each of those can delete old records.

That's why "preserve" includes asking colleagues not to run `git fetch --prune`, `git gc` or a re-clone until you've read their reflogs. Each of those can delete old records.

beats.text: Severity. Severity decides who is told and how fast, not how interesting the Git problem is. The textbook's scale is a working scale for repository incidents, to be adapted to your organisation's own. It asks three questions: which state was affected, could wrong code or a secret have reached users or outsiders, and is anything unrecoverable.
beats.tele: Severity. Severity decides who is told and how fast, not how interesting the Git problem is. The textbook's scale is a working scale for repository incidents, to be adapted to your organisation's own. It asks three questions: which state was affected, could wrong code or a secret have reached users or outsiders, and is anything unrecoverable.

beats.text: Three rules for using a scale. Assign the level on what could have happened in the window, not only on what did. Raise the level the moment a secret is involved. Lowering it later costs nothing. And never let severity depend on who caused the incident.
beats.tele: Three rules for using a scale. Assign the level on what could have happened in the window, not only on what did. Raise the level the moment a secret is involved. Lowering it later costs nothing. And never let severity depend on who caused the incident.

beats.text: Quick quiz on the first rule. A production branch was rewritten, and nothing shipped. A, SEV 4. B, SEV 3. Or C, SEV 2? Your answer?
beats.tele: Quick quiz on the first rule. A production branch was rewritten, and nothing shipped. A, SEV 4. B, SEV 3. Or C, SEV 2? Your answer?

beats.text: C. The first rule is the one people resist. The textbook's example is exactly this, a rewritten production branch that shipped nothing and is still SEV 2, because the only thing between the rewritten branch and production was one check.
beats.tele: C. The first rule is the one people resist. The textbook's example is exactly this, a rewritten production branch that shipped nothing and is still SEV 2, because the only thing between the rewritten branch and production was one check.

beats.text: The ten incidents. Each is a directory under incidents/ with three files.
beats.tele: The ten incidents. Each is a directory under `incidents/` with three files.

beats.text: The report is incomplete and partly wrong, as real reports are. The generator is the answer and is read last.

beats.text: The ten-part format. The textbook uses the same ten headings for every incident, and so should your notes: symptoms, evidence, hypotheses, diagnostic commands, root cause, safe recovery, verification, prevention, communication, postmortem. A postmortem is the written record of how the system allowed the incident.

The textbook uses the same ten headings for every incident, and so should your notes: symptoms, evidence, hypotheses, diagnostic commands, root cause, safe recovery, verification, prevention, communication, postmortem. A postmortem is the written record of how the system allowed the incident.

beats.text: Why the solution comes last. The value of a drill is the diagnosis you make without help. Once you've read the cause, that drill can't be repeated. A diagnosis you've read can't be made again.
beats.tele: Why the solution comes last. The value of a drill is the diagnosis you make without help. Once you've read the cause, that drill can't be repeated. A diagnosis you've read can't be made again.

beats.text: The textbook's analogy is a ward doctor with an unstable patient. The doctor follows a fixed sequence: stabilise, record, diagnose, treat, confirm, hand over. The sequence exists because under pressure people skip to treatment.
beats.tele: The textbook's analogy is a ward doctor with an unstable patient. The doctor follows a fixed sequence: stabilise, record, diagnose, treat, confirm, hand over. The sequence exists because under pressure people skip to treatment.

beats.text: The analogy breaks in two places, both in your favor. A repository can be copied in seconds, so a treatment can be rehearsed on a copy. And Git almost never destroys committed work by itself, so "stabilise" usually means stopping people, not stopping a process.
beats.tele: The analogy breaks in two places, both in your favor. A repository can be copied in seconds, so a treatment can be rehearsed on a copy. And Git almost never destroys committed work by itself, so "stabilise" usually means stopping people, not stopping a process.

beats.text: That second point changes what the first minute looks like. In most Git incidents the first act is a sentence, not a command: "Nobody pushes to or resets this branch until I say so." The textbook's production example is exactly that: an ML platform team deploys an inference service from a branch called production, the deploy job refuses to run, and stage 1 is one sentence in the channel.

beats.text: Look at "has not fetched yet". A clone that hasn't fetched is a witness: it still holds the server's old state. Look at "no reflog of its own". And follow the long arrow at the bottom: communication starts at stage 1.

beats.text: Every sandbox has the same layout.
beats.tele: Every sandbox has the same layout.

beats.text: You're allowed to look into and work in every clone, the way you would sit down at a colleague's machine during an incident. git -C ../ravi <command> runs a command in Ravi's clone without leaving yours. You're also the administrator of server.git. Two read-only commands to orient yourself in any sandbox are git ls-remote origin, for what the server holds, and git branch, in each clone.

beats.text: The generator runs with the fixed lab clock, so the commit IDs in your sandbox equal the IDs printed in the solutions and in Chapter 30. Commits that you create in the lab shell use the real clock and get other IDs. Running the generator again deletes the sandbox and builds it afresh. Do that whenever a repair went wrong: an incident sandbox is the one place where a destructive mistake costs nothing.

beats.text: How to solve one. Seven steps, from the README. Read the symptoms and write the symptom in one sentence without interpretation. Collect evidence with read-only commands only, in each clone that matters. Write at least three hypotheses and the command that tells them apart. Preserve before you change. Choose the fix that destroys least and run it one command at a time. Verify with the commands that showed the problem. And write the four lines a CTO needs. There are the four answers from the opening.

beats.text: How to check.
beats.tele: How to check.

beats.text: The check prints one line per condition and ends with PASS, exit status 0, or NOT YET, exit status 1. A check verifies the state you were asked to reach, not the route you took. It can't verify the parts of an incident that aren't Git state, such as rotating a credential or telling the team.
beats.tele: The check prints one line per condition and ends with `PASS`, exit status 0, or `NOT YET`, exit status 1. A check verifies the state you were asked to reach, not the route you took. It can't verify the parts of an incident that aren't Git state, such as rotating a credential or telling the team.

beats.text: The symptom is the report: Ravi's git log no longer lists the commits he made on Friday, and he thinks git pull ate them. That's what a colleague believes. It isn't a diagnosis.
beats.tele: The symptom is the report: Ravi's `git log` no longer lists the commits he made on Friday, and he thinks `git pull` ate them. That's what a colleague believes. It isn't a diagnosis.

beats.text: A failing check has this shape. The script prints one line per condition, each beginning with ok or FAIL, and it ends with NOT YET, the number of failed checks and exit status 1. Each FAIL line names something the recovery was supposed to keep or restore.
beats.tele: A failing check has this shape. The script prints one line per condition, each beginning with `ok` or `FAIL`, and it ends with `NOT YET`, the number of failed checks and exit status 1. Each `FAIL` line names something the recovery was supposed to keep or restore.

beats.text: Stop here, with one prediction for your notes. Which row of today's evidence table will matter most for Ravi's missing commits? Write it down.
beats.tele: Stop here, with one prediction for your notes. Which row of today's evidence table will matter most for Ravi's missing commits? Write it down.

beats.text: I won't confirm it. The repository will. Don't run the replay of Incident 1 and don't open its solution. Generate the incident and find out from the repository what happened. That's your exercise before the next video.

beats.text: Two things differ from real life, and the README says so. The clock, as explained. And the server: a bare repository has no Activity view, no pull requests, no rulesets and no Support desk, all of which belong to GitHub. Where an incident depends on one of those, the solution says what the GitHub-side step is, described from GitHub's documentation.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Skipping to recovery. Root cause: under time pressure the destructive shortcut looks like progress, and the loop exists to delay it until the state is known and preserved.
beats.tele: Skipping to recovery. Root cause: under time pressure the destructive shortcut looks like progress, and the loop exists to delay it until the state is known and preserved.

beats.text: Waiting for the root cause before the first message. Root cause: communication is treated as the end of the loop, when the team needs to know at once which branch to leave alone.
beats.tele: Waiting for the root cause before the first message. Root cause: communication is treated as the end of the loop, when the team needs to know at once which branch to leave alone.

beats.text: Rating severity by what happened to happen. Root cause: the window is ignored; the level depends on what could have reached users or outsiders while the state was wrong.
beats.tele: Rating severity by what happened to happen. Root cause: the window is ignored; the level depends on what could have reached users or outsiders while the state was wrong.

beats.text: Letting colleagues "clean up" their clones. Root cause: a server keeps no reflog, so the history of a server-side branch exists only in the clones, and a pruning fetch, a git gc or a re-clone deletes it.
beats.tele: Letting colleagues "clean up" their clones. Root cause: a server keeps no reflog, so the history of a server-side branch exists only in the clones, and a pruning fetch, a `git gc` or a re-clone deletes it.

beats.text: Reading the generator or the solution first. Root cause: the drill trains diagnosis from an incomplete report, and a cause that has been read cannot be diagnosed again.
beats.tele: Reading the generator or the solution first. Root cause: the drill trains diagnosis from an incomplete report, and a cause that has been read cannot be diagnosed again.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. An ML platform team deploys an inference service from the branch production. On a Tuesday the deploy job refuses to run, with a message that the deployed commit isn't an ancestor of the branch. In plain words, the branch's history no longer contains it.

beats.text: The engineer on call does three things in the first five minutes, and none of them is a repair. Stage 1: one sentence in the channel, "Nobody pushes to or resets production until I say so." Stage 2: she asks two colleagues not to fetch, prune or re-clone, because their clones are the witnesses, and she anchors the commits she can already name, giving each a branch of its own.

beats.text: Stage 6, early: a first status to the lead, with the level. She rates it SEV 2 although nothing was deployed, and says why: the only thing between the rewritten branch and production was one check.

beats.text: The diagnosis, the recovery and the verification come after that, in that order. The lead later says that the first sentence was the most valuable act of the incident: while it stood, nobody added a second problem to the first.

beats.text: Answer out loud. The question has two halves and a constraint. For the rating, a strong answer states the rule it applied and the fact that satisfies it: what stood between the wrong state and production during the window. For the root cause, two sentences, in words a non-specialist can follow, that name the layer, so that the listener knows whether the fix belongs in a person's habits, in a client setting or in a rule on the platform.

beats.text: An incident is a problem in shared state that others depend on while you are still working out what it is.
beats.tele: An incident is a problem in shared state that others depend on while you are still working out what it is.

beats.text: The loop: stabilise, preserve, diagnose, recover, verify, communicate, prevent; stages 2 and 3 only add refs or read state, and the first message goes out at stage 1.
beats.tele: The loop: stabilise, preserve, diagnose, recover, verify, communicate, prevent; stages 2 and 3 only add refs or read state, and the first message goes out at stage 1.

beats.text: A server keeps no reflog, so colleagues' clones are evidence and must not be pruned, collected or re-cloned.
beats.tele: A server keeps no reflog, so colleagues' clones are evidence and must not be pruned, collected or re-cloned.

beats.text: Severity is rated on what could have happened in the window, is raised at once when a secret is involved, and never depends on who caused it.
